---
title: "AI for Clinicians"
subtitle: "Physician AI Literacy · three days, two hours a day"
toc: false
---

A practical, hands-on course in using AI tools well: in daily practice, in documentation, and in teaching. Most of you already have a chatbot open between patients. This weekend makes that deliberate instead of accidental.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
## The rule for the weekend
**AI drafts. You decide.** Every tool. Every task. All three days.
:::

The course runs online, on Google Meet. You do not need a technical background. You do need a device that can join the call, a browser with a tab for one AI assistant account, and the [setup page](setup.qmd), which takes ten minutes. Nothing in the course depends on any one tool. Every patient is fictional, on the [case cards](reference/case-cards.qmd), and nothing you do here puts a real patient's information into any tool.

## The course

On the call you have three tabs: the call, the **slides** (your instructor pastes the link, and every prompt has a Copy prompt button), and your assistant. You do every step with the instructor. Afterwards, each module has a **handout** with the prompts and checks to keep, and each lab a **lab page** to redo at your own pace. Every day is two hours, a ten-minute break included.

## What you leave with

| | What you can do | How you will know |
|---|---|---|
| **A prompting method** | Write a prompt that gets a usable note, letter, or handout on the first pass, using *role, context, format, constraints* | You put a templated draft beside an untemplated one and check both against the card in [Lab 1](day1/lab1-templates-and-limits.qmd) |
| **A short list of tools** | Say which tool fits which job, which do not fit clinical work, and which you cannot use at all | You run the same question through two tools in Labs 1 and 2 and judge the result yourself |
| **A working check** | Catch AI mistakes before they reach a chart, using three questions and a verification workflow | In [Lab 3](day3/lab3-spot-the-error.qmd) you find what is wrong in an output you did not write |
| **A clear line** | State what never goes into a consumer AI tool, and what to do instead | You work through realistic slips on Day Three, then apply the check to your own output |

## The two sentences everything follows from

> AI drafts. You decide.
>
> Tone is not a signal. A verification step is.

The first is the rule. The second is why the rule needs a habit behind it: these tools sound exactly as sure when they are wrong as when they are right, so you cannot judge an answer by how it reads. Most of Day One teaches you to get a better draft. Most of Days Two and Three teach you to check it.
